airport.name: Ellison Onizuka Kona International Airport at Keāhole

summary: Ellison Onizuka Kona International Airport at Keāhole (KOA) serves as the primary gateway to Hawaii's Big Island west coast, located on a stark lava plain near Kailua-Kona. The airport is named in honor of Ellison Onizuka, a Kailua-Kona native and NASA astronaut who perished aboard Space Shuttle Challenger in 1986. Its open-air, tropical terminal design and shared civilian-military use make it distinctive among U.S. airports.
faqs:
Q: Why is the airport named after Ellison Onizuka?
A: The airport was renamed in 1987 to honor Ellison Onizuka, a Kailua-Kona-born astronaut who was one of seven crew members lost in the Space Shuttle Challenger disaster on January 28, 1986.

Q: How far is the airport from Kailua-Kona town?
A: Ellison Onizuka Kona International Airport is approximately 7 miles northwest of downtown Kailua-Kona, typically a 15-20 minute drive along Queen Kaʻahumanu Highway.

Q: Does the airport have open-air terminals?
A: Yes, portions of the terminal feature open-air designs typical of Hawaiian airports, allowing tropical breezes to flow through covered walkways. However, main terminal areas are enclosed and air-conditioned.

Q: Is the airport shared with military operations?
A: Yes, the facility is jointly used as a civilian airport and a military installation, with Coast Guard and other military operations based at the adjacent Ellison Onizuka Memorial Air Station.
transport_tips: Rental cars are the most popular way to reach Kailua-Kona and surrounding resorts, with major agencies located on-site at the airport. Taxi services and rideshares like Uber and Lyft are available, though availability can be limited during peak hours. The Hele-On Bus provides affordable public transit connecting the airport to Kailua-Kona and other Big Island destinations.
local_tip: The airport sits atop a relatively recent lava flow from Hualālai volcano (last erupted around 1801), so look for the stark black lava landscape surrounding the runways—it's a uniquely Hawaiian welcome that you won't see at most airports.
